This upcoming flyby is also a final opportunity to calibrate the spacecraft's instruments before its long cruise phase.

items.blurb: What may look to modern readers like a form of secret code in fact opens the door to a fascinating world of historical music: German lute tablature. As part of an interdisciplinary team of experts, researchers at the University of Bayreuth are now making these sources readable and audible once again through a digital scholarly edition platform.

items.title: Why molecular cage catalysts show enormous differences in performance
items.blurb: Chemistry researchers have developed a new way to identify and understand highly effective artificial enzyme-like catalysts using powerful "molecular cages" that mimic the behavior of nature's enzymes. These tiny, hollow molecular structures act like miniature reaction chambers to trap molecules and accelerate chemical reactions. The cages showed enormous differences in performance, with the best catalysts more than 10,000 times more active than the least effective ones.

items.title: DESTINY model tracks molecular chemistry on uneven, ice-covered grains in interstellar space
items.blurb: Interstellar space is the scene of active chemical processes: molecules form there in the gas, but also on the surface of tiny dust grains covered in ice. To better represent what happens on these surfaces, astrophysicists at the University of Liège are proposing a deterministic approach based on Markov chains with absorbing states, a mathematical tool that had not yet been utilized in astrochemistry. The paper is published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

items.title: Substrate rigidity suppresses the NRF2 antioxidant program in breast cancer cells
items.blurb: Matrix stiffness rises as breast tumors progress, but whether rigidity raises or lowers activity of the KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway is contested: work in breast cancer cells places the antioxidant response on soft matrix, while work in liver cancer places response on stiff. We used publicly available transcriptome data to ask the question across laboratories rather than within one system. Of eleven series identified, four dataset arms passed quality criteria fixed before any biological analysis. Across five contrasts spanning three cell lines and two matrix formats, one program responded in the same direction every time: the NRF2 antioxidant battery was lower on the more rigid substrate in all five. In contrast, SLC7A11, the cystine transporter supporting glutathione synthesis, decreased in all five, by up to 6.5-fold. YAP and TEAD targets did not track rigidity, rising on hydrogels and glass but falling on cell-derived matrix. NFE2L2 and its regulators were unchanged, while targets fell in proportion to their dependence on the antioxidant response element, pointing to control after transcription. An unsupervised partition made without reference to any pathway recovered the same program and survived removal of proliferation genes. In 1,097 TCGA and 1,980 METABRIC breast tumors, the matrix proxy was unrelated to the full battery until immune and hypoxic composition were accounted for, after which the same negative direction appeared in both; and a tumor-intrinsic score excluding macrophage-expressed members showed it more directly. Single-cell and spatial tests produced the predicted direction but could not resolve it, due to limited sample size and because the genes carrying the effect are largely undetectable at spot depth. Reduced antioxidant capacity on rigid substrate predicts greater sensitivity to agents killing through lipid peroxidation, a prediction we set out for experimental test.

items.title: Cell-type label errors inflate neighborhood effects and can reverse niche claims in spatial transcriptomics
items.blurb: Niche analyses ask how a cell's neighbors shape its expression beyond its type. The type comes from a label, and labels are imperfect. Here we show that label errors inflate neighborhood effects and can reverse niche claims. A mislabeled cell still expresses its true type, and because cells of a type sit near one another, the neighborhood is credited with what the label misses. Standard practice, which calls labels on the modeled counts and selects cells by them, hid, exaggerated, or reversed this inflation. Labeling one half of each cell's counts and modeling the other revealed it in nearly every population of six datasets. On semi-synthetic colon data, a labeler that over-called one fibroblast subtype reversed claims of the niche method Niche-DE; new draws of the counts and errors spread at random over subtypes almost never did. Our software, nichepeek, reports the direction of this bias in a user's data.

items.title: gPlace: fast, memory-bounded phylogenetic placement with results identical to pplacer
items.blurb: Phylogenetic placement methods such as pplacer attach query sequences to a fixed reference tree, thereby establishing their evolutionary relationships to the reference sequences. These relationships can then be used to infer taxonomic classifications or likely metabolic functions. gPlace is a drop-in replacement for pplacer that produces identical results while reducing memory requirements by >3-fold and computation time by >30-fold under typical usage. These improvements are achieved by storing less data per node and streamlining the calculations used to position each query sequence. gPlace can also run within a user-specified memory limit by processing only a portion of the reference tree at a time. Consequently, it can efficiently place sequences on large reference trees that would be impractical for pplacer to process. We demonstrate the importance of these improvements by evaluating gPlace as a replacement for pplacer in GTDB-Tk and CheckM, two tools widely used in genome-resolved metagenomic studies. gPlace is released under the GNU General Public License v3.0 and is available at https://github.com/cmc-aau/gPlace.

items.title: RIPPLE: learning nucleotide relations in an RNA foundation model
items.blurb: RNA function depends on interactions between nucleotides that can be widely separated in sequence, yet capturing these relationships remains challenging for RNA language models. Existing approaches primarily learn nucleotide relationships implicitly from individual nucleotide reconstruction or rely on external structural information to model nucleotide interactions. Here we introduce RIPPLE, an RNA foundation model that learns to identify and represent sparse, predictively useful nucleotide relationships directly from sequence. Pretrained on 32.4 million RNA sequences, RIPPLE uses pairwise predictive utility to guide relational learning, transferring training-time supervision into a sequence-only model without requiring structural inputs at inference. RIPPLE improves overall performance across five downstream tasks spanning RNA family classification, ribosome loading prediction, secondary-structure prediction, three-dimensional contact prediction, and splice-site recognition. Mechanistic analyses further show that utility-guided learning improves the recovery of informative interactions and enhances the transferability of learned RNA representations.

items.title: High-resolution omics and functional profiling of fatty-acid-driven metabolic modulation reveal enhanced physiological relevance of engineered heart tissues
items.blurb: Background: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hPSC-CMs) hold vast potential for cardiovascular disease modeling and drug discovery, yet their immaturity limits their ability to recapitulate adult cardiac physiology. Three-dimensional engineered heart tissues (3D-EHTs) provide a functional and more physiologically-relevant model for disease modeling and drug screening. However, EHTs typically retain an immature metabolic phenotype. To further enhance maturation, we investigated how fatty acid (FA) supplementation and physiological insulin concentrations influence metabolic maturation and its consequences for cardiac function, pharmacological responses, and hypoxic injury. Methods: The effects of FA and insulin supplementation on 3D-EHT maturation were investigated using an integrated molecular and functional approach. Four medium variations were evaluated through functional tests, calcium handling assays, immunofluorescence, ATP quantification, gene expression analysis, high-resolution proteomics, and metabolomics to relate metabolic remodeling to tissue function and responses to pharmacological and hypoxic challenges. Results: FA supplementation enhanced the metabolic maturation of EHTs, surpassing the maturation achieved with an already highly specialized cardiomyocyte medium. The combination of FA with physiological insulin concentrations promoted a shift toward oxidative metabolism, supported by metabolic profiling and associated molecular changes identified through proteomic analysis. This metabolic remodeling was accompanied by changes in contractile performance and calcium handling, altered responses to clinically relevant pharmacological agents, and increased susceptibility to hypoxic injury. Notably, drug concentration-response relationships shifted toward clinically relevant exposure ranges for several compounds. Together, these findings establish a link between metabolic maturation, molecular remodeling, and functional responses of 3D cardiac tissues to pharmacological and pathological challenges. Conclusions: Our findings demonstrate that metabolic culture conditions influence not only the maturation state of hPSC-CMs in 3D-EHTs but also their responses to drugs and hypoxic stress. By integrating multi-omics profiling with functional and disease-relevant assessments, this study provides a framework for improving the physiological relevance of engineered cardiac tissues for disease modeling and preclinical drug evaluation.

items.title: ONTOLOGY™: Streamlined DNA Barcoding and Metabarcoding on Nanopore
items.blurb: Nanopore sequencers have unlocked the potential for a distributed network of DNA barcoding and metabarcoding laboratories. However, the realization of this potential confronts two challenges--one molecular, one computational. First, rigorous indexing protocols are critical to correctly associate sequences with their source specimen or sample; and second, data interpretation often demands processing millions of indexed reads in a structured fashion via complex bioinformatic pipelines. ONTOLOGY addresses these challenges. At its core lies a graphical user interface (GUI) that guides users through the workflow from specimen or sample reception to the generation of DNA barcode records or metabarcode files. To facilitate data acquisition, it includes freeze-dried PCR plates that uniquely tag the amplicons from each well, hence supporting sample-sequence association. The ONTOLOGY GUI is constructed around two core workflows that process data from a sequencing Run. The Barcode Inference Pipeline (BIP) delineates the OTU(s) recovered from each well and designates them as target or non-target sequences via comparison of OTU sequences to a reference sequence library. The Metabarcoding Analysis Pipeline (MAP) processes sequence arrays derived from bulk samples (organismal or environmental DNA) and infers the species represented while rigorously excluding false positives. To validate ONTOLOGY, we present an original data analysis completed via both pipelines. Built for maximum flexibility, ONTOLOGY also supports the analysis of custom experiments. By employing a GUI to coordinate passage through the workflows with structured amplicon tagging and informatics pipelines, ONTOLOGY facilitates the molecular analyses needed to advance biodiversity science via decentralization. Plates and software can be obtained from www.ontology.bio.

items.title: RepeatViewer: a platform for explorative analysis of repetitive DNAs
items.blurb: RepeatViewer is a graphical user interface application designed for repetitive sequence inspection and curation, especially focusing on, but not limited to, transposable elements (TEs). It automatically identifies structural features of TEs, including long terminal repeats (LTRs), terminal inverted repeats (TIRs), and target side duplications (TSDs). All detected and user-defined annotations can be interactively inspected, edited, and exported. RepeatViewer also integrates a TE curation workflow intended to facilitate their manual refinement. In addition, it provides interactive visualization of TE sequences and genome-wide TE annotations, such as dot plots as well as TE distribution and divergence analyses. RepeatViewer is modularly built and can be easily customized by the user.

items.title: Publicly Available Genomic Evidence for Nipah and Avian Influenza Viruses in Bangladesh: A Scoping Assessment of Metadata Completeness and Surveillance Representativeness at the Human-Animal Interface
items.blurb: Bangladesh experiences recurrent Nipah virus (NiV) outbreaks and sustained avian influenza virus (AIV) activity. Whether public genomic records contain metadata needed to assess surveillance representativeness across hosts, locations, and time is unclear.We conducted a structured, source-based scoping assessment of publicly documented NiV and AIV genomic records from Bangladesh (2001-2025), drawing on NCBI GenBank/INSDC and cited peer-reviewed and public-health sources. A pilot registry contained 108 entries (55 NiV, 53 AIV). Metadata were retained only when explicitly reported; unverified fields were recorded as not extracted. The registry is not a complete census. Five analytical questions were prespecified; several could not be evaluated because accession-level metadata were unavailable. The 33-accession AIV set containing H5N1 and H3N8 was excluded from H5/H9-specific interpretation. In the pilot registry, 9/108 entries (8.3%) had explicitly reported host species; the separate host-implied category was not added. Twelve entries (11.1%) had a full collection date; 21 (19.4%) had any collection date. Eight entries (7.4%) had an explicit district. The registry lists 22 NiV accession identifiers from a 2026 study, whereas the publication reports 23 newly sequenced N-gene records; this remains unresolved. Eight AIV accessions (PV961349.1-PV961356.1) represent eight segments of one chicken H5N1 isolate, not eight genomes. Twelve MN994-series records are HA-gene sequences from environmental live-bird-market samples.The pilot registry demonstrates substantial metadata limitations. Explicit host information was available for 8.3% of entries and explicit district for 7.4%; these prevent reliable quantitative assessment of host, district-level, and temporal representativeness and do not establish absence of surveillance or viral circulation. Accession-level reconstruction with transparent verification tiers and harmonised identifiers is required before quantitative representativeness indices or district-level priorities can be calculated.

items.title: Explaining an early ground-nesting bee emergence with climate and occurrence data: Temperature, not precipitation, advances onset
items.blurb: Understanding the drivers of bee phenology is important for predicting how climate change may alter the temporal overlap between bee activity and plant flowering, with consequences for pollination. We documented unusually early emergence of Melissodes tepidus timberlakei Cockerell, 1926 at a perennial nesting site in spring 2026 and examined the relationship between emergence and climatic conditions with (1) five years of nesting observations at a single site, and (2) 119 years of M. tepidus occurrence records from across the western United States. We found that warming temperatures were associated with earlier emergence, whereas precipitation was not, and we emphasize the utility of monitoring ground nests to understand emergence drivers in bees during ongoing climate change.

items.title: Structural basis for m2,2G27 formation and tRNA remodeling by human TRMT1L
items.blurb: tRNAs acquire complex chemical signatures through ordered maturation pathways in which some enzymes contribute both catalytic and non-catalytic activities. Human TRMT1L installs m2,2G27 in tyrosine tRNA and has been reported to support D-loop acp3U20 formation, but the structural basis connecting these functions is unknown. Here, cryo-electron microscopy and mutagenesis show that TRMT1L is a homodimer that extensively reshapes its tRNA substrate. One protomer clamps the acceptor and T arms and supplies the catalytic pocket, while the other engages the anticodon loop. Charge reversal at these anticodon contacts abolishes methylation without disrupting the dimer, showing that engagement by one protomer is required for catalysis by the other. Cofactor binding is accompanied by reorganization of the D- and anticodon arms that draws G27 into the catalytic pocket. In a second cofactor-bound state an active-site loop (L1) that is disordered without cofactor becomes ordered near the position of the extruded base, suggesting a steric gating mechanism that controls access to the catalytic site. Thus, TRMT1L remodels its substrate rather than closing around it, a property that may explain its requirement for modifications that it does not itself catalyze.

items.title: Human Precision-Cut Kidney Slices as a Translational Platform for Modelling Fibrotic, Inflammatory, Metabolic and Drug-Induced Kidney Injury
items.blurb: Introduction. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is characterised by progressive fibrosis and inflammation. Preclinical models of these processes translate poorly to human CKD. Animal models are limited by species differences, while two-dimensional cultures and organoids do not reproduce the three-dimensional, multicellular environment of the human kidney. We sought to develop and characterise precision-cut human kidney slices (PCKS) as an ex-vivo platform for studying renal disease and testing therapeutics. Methods. PCKS were prepared from human donor kidneys not utilised for transplantation and cultured in a proprietary bioreactor for up to six days. Tissue integrity, fibrogenesis, inflammation, lipid handling, and drug-induced injury were assessed by histology, digital pathology, secreted protein quantification, mass spectrometry-based lipidomics, and bulk RNA sequencing, with and without pharmacological intervention. Results. PCKS retained native cortical architecture and viability throughout culture. Slices underwent spontaneous, time-dependent fibrogenesis that was enhanced by transforming growth factor beta 1, abrogated by an ALK5 inhibitor, and attenuated by nintedanib but not pirfenidone. Single-fibre digital pathology resolved treatment-dependent changes in collagen content, morphology and architecture. Proinflammatory stimuli induced stimulus-selective cytokine and chemokine secretion through NF-{kappa}B, which was suppressed by an IKK2 inhibitor. Fatty acid treatment reproduced features of fatty kidney disease, including triacylglycerol accumulation and dose-dependent inflammation, while nephrotoxic drugs produced characteristic injury detectable across multiple longitudinal readouts. Conclusions. Human PCKS maintain renal architecture and viability ex-vivo and reproduce fibrotic, inflammatory, metabolic, and toxic responses at transcriptomic, proteomic and lipidomic scales. PCKS provide a physiologically relevant, human-based platform for renal disease modeling and drug discovery.

items.title: H19 isoform switching during neuronal differentiation reveals a distinct pluripotency-associated non-canonical transcript
items.blurb: H19 is one of the earliest discovered and most extensively studied lncRNAs, yet most studies have focused on the canonical 2,315-nt transcript arising from the IGF2/H19 locus on chromosome 11. We examined H19 isoform usage during the pluripotency-to-neuronal transition using NGN2/ASCL1-induced neurogenesis in KOLF2.1J human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs). We show that a smaller, non-canonical isoform, variant 3, is the predominant H19 isoform in the pluripotent cells examined. This isoform lacks the large canonical promoter-derived exon 1 and contains a short, unique first exon encoded within the imprinting control region upstream of H19. Upon neuronal induction, isoform-specific RT-qPCR showed that variant 3 declined below the lower limit of reliable quantification (LLRQ) as canonical H19 and IGF2 mRNA increased. In contrast, human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells expressed canonical H19, while variant 3 remained below the LLRQ during neurogenic, osteogenic, and adipogenic differentiation. Independent FANTOM5 CAGE datasets supported transcription initiation in the predicted variant 3 promoter region in hiPSCs and human embryonic stem cells. Long-read RNA-seq identified transcripts linking the variant 3 first exon to downstream H19 exons. Public OCT4 and SOX2 ChIP-seq datasets showed recurrent peak overlap at the upstream OSM1 candidate region in pluripotent cells, with corresponding peaks absent in the differentiated datasets examined. Together, these findings support cell-state-associated regulation of the IGF2/H19 locus and identify alternative H19 isoform usage as a feature of human pluripotent cells.

items.title: Early Corneal Host-Response Signatures Associate with Disease Severity and Etiology-Related Clinical Outcomes in Fungal Keratitis
items.blurb: Background: To advance host-based predictive marker development for individual risk assessment in fungal keratitis (FK), we investigated corneal host-response gene-expression signatures associated with etiology-related disease course and clinical outcomes. Methods: We compared severity, healing, and visual outcomes in 1,304 patients with Fusarium spp., Aspergillus flavus, or culture-negative keratitis. Presentation-stage corneal scrapings from 70 prospective patients underwent bulk RNA sequencing stratified by etiology, severity, and outcome. Candidate signatures were independently validated by RT-qPCR in 102 patients using clinical correlations, individual cutoff-based profiling, and masked testing, followed by experimental evaluation in corneal epithelial and macrophage-like cells challenged with live fungal spores. Results: Fusarium keratitis more frequently healed with preserved vision. A. flavus and culture-negative keratitis had the highest and lowest proportions of severe and unhealed disease, respectively, despite similarly poor visual outcomes among healed patients. Transcriptomics paralleled these patterns, revealing a distinct Fusarium host response but substantial A. flavus-culture-negative concordance. A coordinated 8-gene innate-response module correlated with ulcer size and discriminated severe from non-severe disease (AUC, 0.82-0.96), while showing more robust expression in A. flavus and culture-negative than Fusarium keratitis. Higher corneal ICOSL was associated with healing, whereas increased SLC26A4/pendrin characterized non-healing and visual impairment, particularly in Fusarium keratitis. Together, these formed a 10-gene panel whose cutoff-based profiles showed concordance with severity and outcome in masked testing. Experimental evaluation revealed cell- and pathogen-specific expression patterns consistent with patient profiles. Conclusions: Presentation-stage corneal host-response profiles capture etiology-associated differences in FK severity and outcome and identify a candidate 10-gene framework for individualized risk stratification.

items.title: Toxoplasma gondii-induced NETs are mediated by CR3 engagement and the vital non-lytic NETosis pathway
items.blurb: Approximately one-third of the global human population harbors an infection with the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii. The immune system exploits neutrophils and one of their effector mechanisms, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), as an attempt to capture and neutralize T. gondii. NETs, composed of DNA, myeloperoxidase, citrullinated histone 3, and elastase, play a dual role in pathogen entrapment and amplification of the immune response. Traditionally, NET release was considered to result in neutrophil cell death. However, studies have identified an alternative process, vital NETosis, that allows NET formation while maintaining cell viability. Although T. gondii induces NET formation, the associated molecular mechanisms are not fully understood, and the neutrophil fate is unknown. In this study, the promyelocytic cell line HL-60 was differentiated into neutrophil-like cells (NLCs) and infected with type I (RH) or type II (PA7) T. gondii. Extracellular DNA was found in increasing concentrations over time in both type 1 and type 2 T. gondii-infected NLCs. Immunofluorescence staining for DNA and citrullinated histone 3 at 4, 6, and 16 hours post-infection confirmed NET formation by confocal microscopy. Cell viability at 16 hours post-infection was assessed by live/dead staining and extracellular ATP measurement, revealing that most NET-releasing neutrophils retained membrane integrity, consistent with vital NETosis. Additionally, immunofluorescence microscopy at 15 and 30 minutes further confirmed the fast release of nuclear DNA, a hallmark of vital NETosis. The use of opsonin-containing human serum and an anti-CD11b blocking antibody identified complement receptor 3 (CR3) as a receptor mediating T. gondii-induced vital NETosis. These findings demonstrate that T. gondii triggers vital NETosis in neutrophils through a CR3-dependent mechanism, advancing our understanding of the innate immune response to this globally prevalent parasite and laying the groundwork for future investigations into the molecular pathways that may be therapeutically targeted to support neutrophil-mediated immunity during infection.

items.title: Strain-resolved metagenomics shows gut microbiome signatures in a case-control study of Malawian children with zoonotic schistosomiasis
items.blurb: In 2024, Mangochi District, Malawi, we identified unexpected cases of zoonotic schistosomiasis associated with faecal egg excretion of Schistosoma haematobium, Schistosoma mattheei and hybrids thereof (S. haematobium x S. mattheei). Schistosomiasis is associated with gut microbiome alterations, but these associations remain unexplored in zoonotic schistosomiasis. Whether people with schistosomiasis are colonised with more closely related gut bacterial strains than people without schistosomiasis is also unclear. To better understand these patterns, we conducted a case-control study, using strain-resolved metagenomics to analyse faecal samples from 36 children: 12 with zoonotic schistosomiasis (S. haematobium and S. mattheei), 12 with "classic" urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium only) and 12 uninfected controls. Microbial diversity, taxonomic composition, metabolic pathways and antimicrobial resistance gene profiles did not differ significantly between groups. However, Brachyspira, particularly Brachyspira aalborgi - an organism often associated with intestinal spirochaetosis - was more abundant in children with zoonotic schistosomiasis. We found no evidence of closely related B. aalborgi strains shared between participants, suggesting that localised B. aalborgi transmission networks are unlikely to explain the enrichment. In contrast, phylogenetic profiling across 143 other bacterial species revealed greater strain similarity between the gut microbiomes of children with any type of schistosomiasis than between those of controls. Broadly, we demonstrate the scientific value of strain-resolved metagenomics for investigating linked bacterial and schistosome exposures where local water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure is inadequate. Future inclusion of livestock and environmental samples could be used to better identify where transmission pathways overlap, providing evidence to inform integrated disease surveillance and control.

items.title: Dynamic interactions of the coronavirus PEDV nucleoprotein with its viral partner nsp3 and RNA
items.blurb: Summary While coronavirus genome replication and transcription occur inside double-membrane vesicles (DMVs) in infected cells, nucleocapsid assembly of genomic RNA takes place at their cytoplasmic (external) face. Neosynthesized viral mRNAs (including genomic RNA) are exported from the DMV through nsp3/nsp4 pores and genomic RNAs are believed to be selected for encapsidation through an essential interaction of the nucleoprotein N with the amino-terminal domain of nsp3. Here, we describe the interaction play between the N of porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV, an alphacoronavirus) with the N-terminal domain of nsp3 and with RNAs. While N interacts with the N-terminal domain of nsp3 with a dissociation constant (KD) of about 150 nM, it binds to diverse small RNAs, displaying an affinity in the pM range for a short RNA (RNA[8mer]). This RNA and a 60-nt long RNA hairpin were both able to fully displace nsp3 complexed with N. In contrast, nsp3 was not able to dissociate RNA from N-RNA complexes. Using truncated forms of N and of the N-ter domain of nsp3, we showed that the RNA binding site does not fully overlap the nsp3 binding site on N. These results suggest that the interaction play between N, nsp3 and RNA is unidirectional, allowing to propose a mechanistical model for genome encapsidation, model in which N is first recruited by nsp3 at the cytoplasmic face of the DMV to bind to nucleotide stretches of (genomic) RNA exiting from the nsp3/nsp4 channel and concomitantly to dissociate from nsp3.

items.title: CurveKinetix: A user-friendly application for analysis of biological time series data
items.blurb: Of interest to many biologists is how organisms change over time: their growth, their response to a stimulus, their movement. How quickly a process starts, accelerates, slows, or changes direction, often carries critical biological information for hypothesis testing. Extraction of these parameters, however, requires computational expertise or reliance on existing software not designed for the needed analysis. We present here CurveKinetix, a graphical user interface application that helps researchers extract quantitative parameters from time series data without writing code. Users can quickly go from instrument data files to estimation of parameters using three complementary methods to visualized data customization and export. We exhibit CurveKinetix's utility in two case studies. In the first, we show expression of an operon correlates with slowing of population level growth. In the second, we enumerate viral fusion dynamics, demonstrating CurveKinetixs framework can be applied to a range of biological questions. By making flexible quantitative analysis straightforward, CurveKinetix helps experimentalists extract more information from their data and supports clearer, more rigorous interpretation of time-resolved experiments.

items.title: Olfactory epithelium local proteomic during SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters
items.blurb: SARS-CoV-2 has been extensively studied since its recent emergence. It has proven to be an excellent model of respiratory virus impact on nasal epithelium for its massive impact notably on the olfactory epithelium using the hamster animal model. We and others have previously observed that following infection, the nasal epithelium is massively infiltrated by innate immune cells followed by desquamation leading to release of cellular debris in the lumen of the nasal cavity. This impact varies spatially in the nasal cavity, the anterior part being infected early mainly in the respiratory epithelium followed by the olfactory epithelium in the posterior part. In order to better understand the impact on host cells, we decided to use laser microdissection to analyse the proteomic of restricted area of infected epithelium taking into account this spatial variation. We observed that protein levels are mostly decreased following SARS-CoV-2 infection at 2 days post-infection which contrasts with many genes having a stable expression level. Using available scRNASeq library, we could associate the variation of protein levels to the various cell types of the nasal cavity epithelium and our findings are consistent with a destruction of most epithelial cells and the infiltration of innate immune cells. Overall, our study confirms that SARS-CoV-2-host interactions lead to profound alteration of genes expression and that while most studies heavily rely on mRNA levels, it may be decorrelated to protein levels. Our approach offers an alternative to study host-virus interactions using spatially restricted proteomic.

items.title: Calcium Signaling and Glycerol-3-Phosphate Metabolism Coordinate Extracellular Vesicle Biogenesis in Cryptococcus neoformans
items.blurb: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly recognized as important mediators of fungal physiology and host-pathogen interactions, but the mechanisms governing their biogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we combined time-course RNA sequencing with genome-wide genetic screening to define the regulatory network controlling EV production in the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. Transcriptomic analysis identified an EV-associated regulon enriched in genes involved in vesicular trafficking, cell wall remodeling, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function and ion homeostasis. Our screen further identified diverse regulators of EV production, highlighting endosomal trafficking, mitochondrial metabolism and calcium homeostasis. Cell viability was only weakly associated with EV production, arguing against cell lysis as the primary mechanism of EV release. Genetic and pharmacological analyses established calcium-dependent calcineurin signalling as a major regulator of EV production. We identified the calcineurin target Had1 as a positive regulator of EV production and demonstrate that Had1 functions as a glycerol-3-phosphate phosphatase. Loss of HAD1 caused glycerol-3-phosphate accumulation and extensive remodeling of cellular phospholipids, accompanied by a marked reduction in EV production. Together, these findings identify a calcium-calcineurin-Had1 pathway linking intracellular signalling and lipid homeostasis to fungal EV biogenesis.

items.title: Global evolutionary and spatiotemporal transmission dynamics of human respiroviruses and orthorubulaviruses
items.blurb: Human parainfluenza viruses (HPIVs) cause recurrent epidemics and are a major cause of hospitalization worldwide. However, the evolutionary and transmission dynamics driving HPIV persistence remain unclear. We analysed 1,161 archived samples representing four HPIV types from seven countries using genomic sequencing and Bayesian phylodynamic inference. We show that Respirovirus (HRV-1 and HRV-3) displayed greater fluctuations in genetic diversity whereas Orthorubulavirus (HOV-2 and HOV-4) showed more gradual changes. Despite comparable evolutionary rates, the four HPIV types exhibited contrasting lineage dynamics. HRV-1 showed prolonged lineage persistence, HRV-3 underwent greater lineage turnover, and HOV-2 and HOV-4 maintained fewer co-circulating lineages. Positive selection was more pronounced in respiroviruses, particularly in the phosphoprotein gene, while positively selected sites overlapped predicted hemagglutinin-neuraminidase B-cell epitopes. Phylogeographic analyses revealed repeated interregional introductions, bidirectional transmission, and regional persistence exceeding a decade for some lineages. These findings identify distinct evolutionary and transmission dynamics underlying HPIV persistence and inform the development of broadly protective vaccines and therapeutics.

items.title: A tricomponent mRNA pertussis vaccine elicits superior protective immunity over licensed acellular pertussis vaccine against emerging antibiotic-resistant variants
items.blurb: Pertussis remains a major global health burden and has been resurging rapidly over the past decade. The causes of pertussis re-emergence are multifactorial, including vaccine-induced pathogen evolution, antimicrobial resistance, and crucially suboptimal protective immunity elicited by the widely used acellular pertussis vaccine (aPV). In this study, we developed a tricomponent mRNA pertussis vaccine formulated with lipid nanoparticle (LNP), designated mPervax, which encodes inactive pertussis toxin subunit 1 (PTS1), truncated filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA) and pertactin (PRN). Compared to a commercialized Tetanus-diptheria-pertussis vaccine Boostrix, mPervax induced stronger and broader innate immune activation, superior antigen-specific Th1-type CD4+ T and Tfh cell responses, and robust B. pertussis-specific antibody responses with remarkably increased magnitude and functionality. In addition, mPervax conferred an efficient maternal antibody-mediated protection in offspring mice and reshaped the immune profile established by primary Boostrix immunization towards a Th1-phenotype when used as a heterologous booster. Furthermore, upon bacterial challenge, mPervax outperformed Boostrix not only against the WHO reference strain 18323, but strikingly provided effective protection against emerging antibiotic-resistant clinical isolates that are deficient in PRN and/or FHA. Collectively, these data demonstrate that the mRNA pertussis vaccine is superior to Boostrix in multiple contexts, and therefore holds promise for next-generation pertussis vaccine development.

items.title: Elucidating and Overcoming Lignin-Mediated Growth Suppression in Anaerobic Fungi
items.blurb: Native to the gastrointestinal tract of herbivores, anaerobic gut fungi (AGF) (Neocallimastigomycetes) have evolved highly efficient enzymatic machinery for lignocellulose degradation. While AGF are capable of degrading lignocellulose, they more readily degrade its cellulose and hemicellulose components. Lignin is the most recalcitrant component of lignocellulose that serves as both structural support and a microbial defense strategy within plants. In this study, a negative correlation between AGF growth and substrate lignin content was quantified, ranging from pure cellulose to the lignin-rich substrate eucalyptus. Based on this observation, we investigated the impact of lignin on AGF viability and concluded that lignin delayed and slowed AGF?s growth trajectory, with IC50 ranging from 10.7 ? 16.3 mg/mL, and specifically that lignin-rich substrates decreased overall growth. Meanwhile, lignin acted as an AGF deterrent, likely by preventing access to essential sugar-based polymers and lowering overall nutrient bioavailability. However, AGF growth was restored following glucose supplementation on otherwise growth-limiting woody substrates. Through experimental, sequential serial batch culture challenge, we successfully adapted one strain of AGF (Neocallimastix californiae) to grow on lignin-rich eucalyptus. This study supports the industrial valorization of lignocellulose using AGF by elucidating the relationship between the major bottleneck, lignin, on fungal growth. It also provides a strategy for optimizing fungal strains selected for growth in nutrient-deficient and lignin-rich environments.

items.title: Alternative splicing links sex to neutrophil inflammatory vulnerability
items.blurb: Mammalian females generally live longer than males, yet the immunological drivers governing sex-biased inflammatory mortality remain unclear. Neutrophils, among conserved immune cells across species, exhibit marked sex differences in inflammatory and age-related diseases. We identified conserved male-biased CD11b expression in resting neutrophils of wild-type mice, Rag2 KO mice, and in human cohorts. Male neutrophils selectively displayed CD11b-dependent transendothelial migration. During tissue inflammation in our mouse model deficient in -Klotho (Kl) combined with Rag2 KO lymphocyte depletion (dKO), males showed higher mortality and more severe pulmonary pathology correlated with increased infiltrating neutrophils in the lung. The neutrophil accumulation directly accounted for heightened IL-1{beta} expression in males despite equivalent per-cell cytokine expression across sexes. Transcriptomic analysis of neutrophils revealed profound sex-biased alternative splicing enriched in Toll-like receptor (TLR) cascades, alongside hormone-responsive regulation of integrin {beta}2 (Itgb2) isoform usage, implicating alternative splicing in neutrophils represents male vulnerability to tissue inflammation.

items.title: Intravenous BCG Elicits a Sustained Myeloid IFNG Response Signature Associated with Early TB Control
items.blurb: Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) administered intravenously (IV) to rhesus macaques can prevent pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) infection. To establish transcriptional correlates of protection, we generated longitudinal CITE-Seq data across blood and lung after IV BCG in macaques and compared it to clinically approved intradermal (ID) BCG. We define an interferon gamma (IFNG) response signature in alveolar macrophages (AMs) comprising 61 genes with diverging expression between IV and ID BCG from 4 to 16 weeks after vaccination that was also enriched in AMs early after TB challenge. The signature was recapitulated in blood monocytes (IV vs. ID) and associated with protection in an independent cohort of IV BCG-vaccinated macaques. Cell-cell communication analysis inferred increased ligand-receptor interactions in the airway after IV BCG, including those between multiple IFNG-producing T cell subsets and AMs. The sustained IFNG response signature in AMs after IV BCG provides a new correlate and potential mechanism of early TB control informing future vaccine design.

items.title: Cholesterol and high concentration serum cooperatively enhance canine CAR T cell transduction and expansion
items.blurb: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell immunotherapy is emerging as a promising adjunct treatment option for refractory canine cancers. Unfortunately, clinical trials thus far have failed to meaningfully reduce tumor burden, highlighting the need for improved CAR T cell manufacturing strategies. Effective autologous therapy requires highly viable, efficiently transduced T cells capable of robust expansion, sustained CAR expression, and long-term persistence. Although these parameters have been extensively investigated in humans, comparable optimization in canine systems remains limited. Here, we evaluated culture conditions to improve canine T cell expansion, memory differentiation, and retroviral transduction efficiency. We demonstrated IL-2 supplementation supported superior cellular expansion and preservation of less-differentiated memory phenotypes compared to IL-7 with IL-15. Additionally, we found that increasing cell density during shorter stimulation periods improved expansion while also driving better T cell transduction rates. We discovered that the addition of cholesterol and high-concentration fetal bovine serum (FBS) to media during the transduction period reliably and markedly enhanced transduction efficiency following a single round of retroviral transduction, even at elevated temperatures that would otherwise impair transduction efficiency. This enhancement was observed with both GALV- and RD114-pseudotyped retroviruses and was accompanied by a marked improvement in cellular expansion without driving terminal differentiation of T cell subsets that are prone to exhaustion in vivo. Collectively, these findings identify practical strategies to improve canine CAR T-cell manufacturing and advance the development of clinically viable CAR T cells for canine cancer treatment.

items.title: Single cell mapping reveals phenotypic, immunometabolic and functional heterogeneity among age-associated B cells in systemic lupus erythematosus and aging
items.blurb: Abstract/Summary Introduction: Age-associated B cells (ABCs) comprise an antigen-experienced memory B-cell population that expands during aging but has also been implicated in autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Cell immunometabolism has emerged as a key determinant of immune-cell function, linking metabolic adaptation to both protective and maladaptive immunity or pathological inflammation, thereby providing a platform for therapeutic intervention. This study aims to comprehensively profile the functional alterations that accommodate ABC expansion, emphasizing metabolic reprogramming within the B-cell compartment in SLE, particularly with regard to ABCs, in order to identify niche metabolic pathways utilized by ABCs that may represent useful therapeutic targets. Methods: An exploratory analysis was conducted using publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing datasets to phenotypically and functionally characterize ABC populations in patients with SLE and lupus-prone MRL.lpr mice, using a broad array of community tools. We further conducted SCENITH-based metabolic profiling to assess metabolic differences among splenic follicular (FO), marginal zone (MZ) and CD21-CD23- double negative (DN) B cells, in the murine SLE-like MRL.lpr model, in which we tested the ability of B cell subsets to generate protein output, following exposure to specific metabolic inhibitors (2-deoxyglucose and oligomycin). In addition, we cross-examined CD21-CD23- DN B cells in the native context of aging by employing flow cytometry-based analyses of their redox status (NADH/FAD autofluorescence) and mitochondrial function (MitoTracker and TMRE staining) to investigate age-associated metabolic programming. Results: Single-cell transcriptomic analyses revealed substantial immunophenotypic and metabolic heterogeneity within the ABC compartment in SLE. Subclustering of ABCs revealed three separate and distinct ABC subsets, encompassing CD68 ABCs, NKG7 ABCs, and AREG ABCs, differing in their respecrive transcriptional, functional, and immunometabolic signatures. The CD68 ABC subset demonstrated signs of enhanced cytotoxicity, phagocytosis, lysosomal activity, and increased antigen-processing capabilities. The CD68 and NKG7 ABC populations exhibited increased inflammatory pathway activity, including pattern-recognition receptor signalling and NLRP3 inflammasome-associated activity, while the AREG ABC subset displayed signs of senescence, moderation, exhaustion, or anergy. hdWGCNA identified transcriptional modules associated with acetyltransferase activity, suggesting a potential link between metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic remodelling through epimetabolite availability, in particular acetyl-CoA. ABCs demonstrated, in general, coordinated amplification of glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, and lipid utilization, with substantial intragroup metabolic heterogeneity among the three ABC subsets. The CD68 ABCs emerged as the most hypermetabolic subset. In parallel, SCENITH-based metabolic comparison of CD21-CD23- DN B cells between mildly diseased male and severely diseased female MRL.lpr mice revealed increased utilization of alternative non-glucose substrates and enhanced glycolytic activity, but reduced overall protein synthesis capacity, indicating altered allocation of metabolic resources. Further interpretation of the transcriptomic analysis suggests that proteasomal activity could explain the lower protein levels in female MRL.lpr mice, as measured by SCENITH. In addition, in silico drug prediction pointed towards statins and proteasome inhibitors as potentially useful pharmacological agents for blocking cholesterol metabolism and protein degradation, respectively. Finally, the analysis of aged mice also revealed metabolic and redox alterations in ABC-enriched CD21-CD23- DN B cells under physiological aging conditions. Conclusions: Human ABCs appear to comprise a heterogeneous constellation of various subsets possessing different functional properties, as well as different pro-inflammatory or immunoregulatory statuses. ABCs exhibit a distinct hypermetabolic state associated with lupus-related immune dysregulation, but also with aging, in line with previous reports. However, as the disease manifests and progresses, protein production appears to be dampened, which could be attributed to ribosomal problems or proteasome-mediated protein degradation. Metabolic reprogramming is accompanied by enhanced phagocytic and lysosomal programs, which may facilitate the uptake of self-material and contribute to autoreactive immune responses, in particular anti-nuclear autoantibody production. Increased OXPHOS activity may accommodate epigenetic reprogramming towards the atypical memory phenotype displayed by ABCs. Identification of ABC-specific metabolic dependencies may provide opportunities for therapeutic intervention, with lipid consumption being of particular interest. These findings support further investigation of metabolic modulators, including HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors and proteasome-targeting strategies, to limit their pathogenic activity in SLE by exploiting their niche metabolic vulnerabilities, in particular their hypermetabolic state and proteostatic stress.

items.title: Nsg2 deficiency attenuates intestinal inflammation and colitis-associated tumorigenesis through microbiome-dependent metabolic remodeling
items.blurb: Background & Aims Neuron-Specific Gene 2 (NSG2) is a neuronally expressed protein that facilitates excitatory synaptic transmission through the regulation of AMPA receptor trafficking. While its function has been characterized in the central nervous system, whether NSG2 plays a role in enteric neuronal signaling and intestinal pathology has yet to be explored. We therefore investigated whether Nsg2 deficiency modulates intestinal inflammation and tumorigenesis through gut microbiome-dependent mechanisms. Methods Dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis and azoxymethane/DSS-induced colitis-associated cancer (DSS-CAC) models were established in Nsg2-/- and wild-type (WT) mice. Disease severity was evaluated using the disease activity index (DAI), histopathological scoring, and tumor burden assessment. To investigate the potential contribution of the gut microbiota to genotype-associated phenotypes, WT and Nsg2-/- mice were co-housed for six weeks before disease induction. Gut microbial composition and predicted functional pathways were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V3-V4 region) and PICRUSt2, respectively. Results Separately housed Nsg2-/- mice exhibited significantly attenuated DSS-induced colitis, with reduced body weight loss, lower DAI scores, and preserved colonic architecture. In the DSS-CAC model, Nsg2-/- mice developed significantly fewer and smaller tumors with suppressed Wnt/beta-catenin signaling. Under co-housing conditions, no statistically significant differences in colitis severity or tumor burden were detected between genotypes, supporting a possible contribution of the gut microbiota to the phenotypes observed in separately housed mice. 16S rRNA sequencing identified distinct microbial communities in Nsg2-/- mice, characterized by greater alpha diversity and enrichment of protective taxa, including Butyricicoccus and Lachnospiraceae. Functional profiling predicted enrichment of methane metabolism, porphyrin biosynthesis, and one-carbon metabolism pathways. Conclusions Nsg2 deficiency confers protection against intestinal inflammation and colitis-associated tumorigenesis, accompanied by alterations in gut microbial composition and suppression of Wnt/beta-catenin signaling. These findings identify NSG2 as a novel modulator at the intersection of enteric neuronal signaling, gut microbiota, and mucosal immunity, positioning it as a potential therapeutic target for IBD and inflammation-driven colorectal cancer.

items.title: Fibronectin binding and non-canonical transcription factor signature distinguishes lung and bone marrow megakaryocytes
items.blurb: Recent evidence has demonstrated the unique morphology and function of lung megakaryocytes (MKs), yet the source of the differences between lung and bone marrow (BM) MKs remains unclear. While BM MKs are large, polyploid, BM-resident cells primarily known as platelet producing cells, lung MKs are smaller, less polyploid, and known for immunomodulation. To better understand the factors underlying the differences in lung and BM MKs, we developed a flow cytometry method for precise characterization and isolation of MKs using leukocyte exclusion and examination of hematopoietic and canonical MK markers. When MK-leukocyte aggregates are excluded, a single femur+tibia contains approximately 1,493 MKs and a single lung contains approximately 4,541 MKs. Enrichment via positive selection efficiently removes unwanted cells, increasing the percentage of MKs amongst live lung cells by 10.29-fold and the percentage of MKs amongst live BM cells by 29.09-fold. Sorted MKs were viable and spread onto fibrinogen. Gene expression analysis demonstrated that lung MKs increase immune pathway gene expression, including TNFRSF1B. Transcription factor (TF) and cell cycle gene expression decreased in lung MKs compared to BM MKs, including reduced expression of GATA1 and CDC6, possibly explaining observations of low ploidy and size in lung MKs, while expression of the TF ETS2 increased. Lung MKs also express increased ITGA4 compared to BM MKs, abundant surface integrin 4 protein, and increased surface integrin {beta}7 protein compared to BM MKs. Additionally, lung MKs bind significantly more fibronectin ex vivo then BM MKs. These data demonstrate for the first time that lung MKs have a unique TF signature and suggests integrin 4{beta}7 as a relevant receptor for lung MK function.

items.title: The metacognitive signatures of imposterism
items.blurb: The imposter phenomenon (or imposterism) is a commonly reported psychological pattern in which individuals persistently doubt their abilities and accomplishments despite objective evidence of their competence. Imposterism is associated with chronic self-doubt and reduced well-being, yet its cognitive mechanisms remain unclear. In a large online sample (N = 602), we investigated how self-reported imposter feelings relate to decision-making, confidence and information search in a perceptual decision-making task. Imposterism was associated with lower confidence in perceptual decisions and increased information seeking, despite not being associated with any detriment in objective perceptual performance. Though symptoms of anxiety and depression contributed to the relationship between imposterism and confidence, imposterism uniquely predicted increased information-seeking. Interestingly, the increased information seeking associated with imposterism did not lead to an imposterism-specific increase in final decision performance and did not alleviate overall uncertainty: imposterism remained associated with reduced confidence even for final decisions. To explain this, we hypothesised that information seeking may compensate for maladaptive second-guessing. Supporting this, imposterism predicted greater response switching and decreases in accuracy on trials where no additional information was sought, reflecting counterproductive changes of mind. These effects were absent on trials where information was accessed, suggesting that seeking additional information helped buffer against maladaptive second-guessing. Overall, our findings show that imposterism is marked by low confidence, heightened information seeking, and vulnerability to second-guessing in the absence of external reassurance. These results provide novel insights into distortions of self-evaluation in imposterism and highlight a compensatory role for information seeking in stabilising performance. Our study advances understanding of a widely discussed yet underexplored psychological phenomenon with significant implications for education, workplace wellbeing, and mental health.

items.title: The Developing Human Connectome Project: Fetal Data Release
items.blurb: The Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP) represents a large open science resource designed to enable detailed investigations of typical and atypical brain development across the perinatal period. It consists of 1228 multimodal magnetic resonance image examinations of the fetal and/or neonatal brain from 1173 participants, together with collateral demographic, clinical, family, neurocognitive and genomic data. All subjects were studied in utero and/or soon after birth with a single MRI scanner using specially developed scanning sequences with novel motion-tolerant imaging methods and optimised for the changing properties of the developing brain. The neonatal data has been described and released separately. The fetal data release consists of multimodal data from 273 subjects scanned between 20 + 6 and 38+2 weeks (+days) of gestation, with some fetuses imaged more than once to provide longitudinal data creating 297 datasets in total. The data include: high resolution and motion corrected T1 and T2 weighted anatomical images; high temporal resolution functional and multi-shell high angular resolution diffusion MRI; and multimodal age-resolved atlases; together with demographic, family and clinical data, genomic and epigenomic data and follow-up neurodevelopmental assessment at around 18 months. This paper describes the dHCP fetal image acquisition, reconstruction and processing protocols, summarizes the available data, and provides information on how it can be accessed.

• Third straight draw leaves title match at 1½–1½

  • Sindarov drops to eight seconds on move 39

  • Gukesh Dommaraju plays white after first rest day

  • All your Gukesh v Sindarov questions, answered

After two quieter draws, the world chess championship came to life on Thursday as Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov came within eight seconds of sudden death before fighting back to split the point with India’s Gukesh Dommaraju after nearly five hours. Their spirited 60-move battle at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs left their $2.5m match level at 1½–1½ heading into the first rest day.

Gukesh, playing with the black pieces, returned to the Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez, the opening he used in Tuesday’s 38-move opener. The defending champion sprang the first surprise on move five (5 … Be7), bringing out his bishop before retreating the knight that had taken Sindarov’s e-pawn, putting the challenger behind on time for the first time in the match. After 15 moves, Gukesh still had nearly 1hr 58min of his starting two hours, almost 40 minutes more than his opponent.

items.title: World: Waiting to tackle HIV in the Pacific could double the cost and prevent fewer infections
items.blurb:
Countries: World, Fiji, Papua New Guinea
Source: Australian National University

Caroline van Gemert

Anna Bowring

Jason Mitchell

Donald Wilson

Across the Pacific, communities are confronting growing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) outbreaks at a time when health budgets are constrained and international development assistance is increasingly uncertain. Fiji has one of the fastest-growing HIV epidemics globally, with new infections rising approximately twelvefold between 2010 and 2025. Papua New Guinea has declared a national HIV crisis, while several other Pacific Island countries and territories are now reporting early warning signs of increased transmission.

When responding to an HIV outbreak, when to invest, how much to invest and what to invest in all shape outcomes. The challenge is not only to secure enough funding, but to make sure it reaches the right people and arrives early enough to change the course of an outbreak.

To examine these trade-offs, we used Optima HIV, a mathematical and economic modelling tool that has been applied around the world to identify how HIV resources can be allocated to minimise new infections and HIV-related deaths.

We modelled a hypothetical Pacific Island country of 100,000 people with an emerging HIV outbreak, using regional epidemiological, behavioural, service and cost data. We compared current approaches with an optimised response: treatment and adherence support for people already diagnosed, plus targeted prevention and testing for key populations. Key populations are the groups most affected by HIV, such as men who have sex with men and people who inject drugs, and they often have limited access to services. We tested this response across several outbreak profiles, starting in either 2027 or 2030.

Four findings emerged: act early, prioritise treatment and adherence support for people already diagnosed, focus prevention and testing on key populations and expect costs to rise before they fall.

First, acting early costs less and prevents more infections. Doubling existing annual HIV investment from 2027 (from about USD32,700 to USD65,500 per 100,000 population per year) and optimising the response was projected to avert more than 90% of new infections by 2040, compared with continuing current approaches. Delaying this response until 2030 would cost on average USD132,500 per 100,000 population per year to achieve a similar result — about twice the annual cost of investing from 2027 — yet would avert fewer infections (86%).

The difference in effectiveness and cost between an early and a delayed response comes down to how HIV spreads. Transmission compounds over time, so an infection prevented today also prevents infections further along the chain. As an outbreak accelerates, a much larger investment is needed just to regain lost ground.

Second, maximising treatment engagement and outcomes among people who are diagnosed is the priority. In the model, scaling up treatment, engagement in care and adherence support did the most to increase viral suppression and prevent onward transmission. Fiji shows why this matters: only 56% of reported people living with HIV were receiving antiretroviral treatment at the end of 2025, and only 15% of those on treatment had documented viral suppression, meaning the virus had been reduced to a level that prevents onward transmission. Coverage across all people estimated to be living with HIV in Fiji, including those not yet diagnosed, is lower still: Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS puts it at about 22%.

Third, prevention and testing should focus first on key populations. Testing and prevention services designed for these groups had a bigger impact than generalised testing and condom programs, because this is where the virus spreads.

Fourth, spending rises first, then falls. Reported diagnoses reveal only part of an outbreak. In our model, around 31% of people living with HIV were diagnosed in 2025, so expanded testing finds many more people who need treatment and adherence support, and that raises costs in the short term. But as future infections are prevented, those projected needs decline. Within about a decade, an optimised response was projected to need fewer treatment and adherence resources than continuing with current approaches.

Together, the findings show countries do not need to wait to deliver a perfect HIV response. Where resources are limited, starting with the interventions most likely to interrupt transmission, then expanding as resources and capacity grow, is more effective than delaying action.

This is not an argument for less HIV funding in the Pacific. It is an argument for targeted investment. Additional domestic and development-partner investment is critical. The finding is that the timing of investment can be just as consequential as its size.

These findings are not a prescription for any individual Pacific country. Local epidemiology, service costs, practical constraints and equity priorities must shape how governments invest. Country-specific Optima models can be built using national epidemiological and program data, with local priorities in mind, and we would welcome the chance to work with ministries and partners to do so.

Which key populations to reach first depends on the outbreak, and in many Pacific countries it is not yet clear what is driving the rise in infections or which populations are affected. Transmission patterns differ between countries and change over time, so we modelled different outbreak profiles, including varying sexual and injecting drug-use-related risks. Without a clear picture of who is most affected, governments cannot be sure where to direct scarce resources. That is why better surveillance data matters: timely local data on who is being infected, and whether they are reaching care, is what allows countries to target their response and adjust it as the outbreak changes.

For governments and development partners, the priority should be to secure effective funding before transmission accelerates, to protect services that reach key populations, to support people to start and stay on treatment and to ensure programs can adapt to local needs. Sustained investment, strong surveillance, better case monitoring and sound epidemiological data are crucial to directing resources as outbreak patterns change.

Pacific governments have already signalled where they want to go. At the 17th Pacific Heads of Health meeting in Rarotonga in August 2026, heads of health accepted two recommendations.

The first is that every Pacific Island country and territory develop or strengthen a national HIV preparedness and response plan within 12 months, including functional HIV surveillance and real-time early-warning indicators. The second is that a Pacific HIV Regional Support Mechanism be established within 18 months. These measures provide a foundation for the kind of early, targeted and sustained investment supported by our modelling. The commitments have been agreed. What they need now is resourcing.

HIV transmission does not pause while budgets are negotiated. The cost of waiting is paid twice: in preventable infections today, and in the greater resources needed to control outbreaks tomorrow.

The authors would like to acknowledge the contributions of Burnet Head of Modelling and Biostatistics, Associate Professor Nick Scott, and Burnet Head of Public Health, Professor Mark Stoové, for their modelling and expertise underpinning this post.

items.title: One Girl Married Every Three Seconds as World Falls Behind on Promise to End Child Marriage
items.blurb:
Countries: World, Bangladesh, occupied Palestinian territory, Sierra Leone
Source: Save the Children

LONDON/GENEVA, 27 November 2026 – Nearly one girl every three seconds is married before the age of 18 despite world leaders committing more than 10 years ago to end child marriage by 2030, said Save the Children said on the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage[1] [2].

Save the Children said progress at ending child marriage has slowed to a crawl, leaving millions of girls at risk of being denied their childhoods, education, safety and future opportunities.

Global child marriage rates have fallen by just 3.4 percentage points since 2014, from 21.9% to 18.5%, and have barely shifted in the last two years [3]. At the current pace, the world is dangerously off track to meet its commitment to end child marriage in the next four years with hard-won gains at risk of reversal, said the child rights organisation.

The warning comes as conflict, climate shocks, displacement, economic pressures and shrinking international aid budgets push more families towards negative coping mechanisms including marrying off their daughters.

According to the Girls Not Brides network, of which Save the Children is a member, 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 each year – around 23 girls married every minute, or 1 girl married every 3 seconds.

In Gaza, latest UN data reveals a significant rise in early and forced marriages incidents, with a stark 123% increase between the first two quarters of 2026. While most reported incidents (67%) involved women aged 18- 59, girls aged 12-17 accounted for 16% of cases.

Despite the alarming slowdown in progress, Save the Children said countries that have invested consistently in girls’ rights and protection demonstrate that change is possible.

In Bangladesh, for example, while nearly half the country’s women aged 20 to 24 were married before age 18, of child marriage rates fell from 62.7% to 47.2% over roughly the same period that global progress stagnated [4]. This was due to no single initiative but sustained political commitment and targeted investments in social protection, girls' education, community-led norm change, prevention and response to gender-based violence, and initiatives that strengthened girls' agency and ability to exercise their rights.

Sierra Leone has also demonstrated how sustained advocacy and political commitment can drive progress. Recently, years of advocacy led by girls, communities, civil society organisations and development partners helped secure stronger legal protections for girls, including the adoption of the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2024. Since then, the 2026 “Never Before 18” campaign, supported by Save the Children, has helped maintain public and political attention on ending child marriage by elevating girls' voices, raising awareness of the law, and calling for its effective implementation across the country.

Rahinatu Adamu Hussaini, Save the Children’s Global Senior Advisor on gender-based violence prevention and response, said:

“Child marriage is not a cultural inevitability or a rite of passage It's a deadline imposed on a girl before she's had the chance to write her own story. It's both a harmful practice, and a form of gender-based violence that violates girls' rights to education, health, bodily autonomy and freedom from violence.

“Yet today, nearly one girl every three seconds is married before the age of 18, forced into a harmful practice that cuts short her childhood, limits her choices, and increases her risk of violence, poor health outcomes and lifelong inequality.

“That's why this new international day matters. It reminds us that behind every statistic is a girl whose rights, aspirations and future are at stake, at a time when progress is stalling and investment in proven solutions is under threat.

" The good news is that we know what works. Child marriage declines when governments invest in girls' education, strengthen social protection systems, prevent and respond to gender-based violence, and create opportunities for girls to participate in decisions that affect their lives.

"Countries such as Bangladesh have shown that progress is possible when commitments are matched with sustained investment and accountability. The challenge before us is not a lack of solutions; it is ensuring those solutions reach the girls who need them most."

Save the Children is urging governments, donors and international institutions to urgently step up funding for solutions that are proven to reduce child marriage, including education for girls, support for vulnerable families, protection from violence, and opportunities for girls to shape their own futures.

Every girl, everywhere, should be able to decide if, when and whom to marry, and to grow up free from violence, coercion and discrimination.

NOTES:

[1] According to the Girls Not Brides network, of which Save the Children is a member, 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 each year – around 23 girls married every minute, or 1 girl married every 3 seconds.

[2] On 4 September 2026, the United Nations General Assembly adopted resolution A/RES/80/309, proclaiming 27 November as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage. The resolution recognizes that these practices violate, abuse or impair human rights and disproportionately affect women and girls, particularly those in vulnerable situations. They can threaten access to education, health, economic opportunities and the full enjoyment of human rights.

[3] UNICEF Global Database on Child Marriage / Save the Children Child Atlas data on Child Marriage

[4] UNICEF Global Database on Child Marriage / Save the Children Child Atlas (According to UNICEF data, the proportion of women aged 20-24 in Bangladesh who were married before age 18 declined from 62.7% to 47.2%, demonstrating significant progress despite continued challenges. The latest estimate of 47.2% comes from the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025.
