items.title: Update 377 – IAEA Director General Statement on Situation in Ukraine
items.blurb:
Country: Ukraine
Source: International Atomic Energy Agency

The IAEA is engaging with the Russian Federation and Ukraine on arrangements for a ninth localized ceasefire at the Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) following another loss of offsite power.

The plant’s connection to its sole remaining external power line, the 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 line, was lost on 25 November at 05:28 local time, reportedly due to military activity. For the 28th time during the conflict, ZNPP is relying on emergency diesel generators for essential nuclear safety and security functions.

“Once again we are faced with a loss of offsite power at the ZNPP. Its continued reliance on a single power line, together with the plant’s location on the front line of an active warzone, results in an extremely precarious offsite power connection,” said IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi.

“I call on both sides to work constructively with the IAEA to cease military activity against electrical infrastructure, facilitate repair of the Ferosplavna-1 line and re-establish an offsite power connection to the ZNPP,” said Director General Grossi.

This event further underscores the importance of negotiations to facilitate repair of the Dniprovska 750 kV power line and its associated substation. The substation was reportedly damaged during military activity in May. The power line was repaired under the sixth Agency-negotiated temporary localized ceasefire in June, but further damage was subsequently identified. The Dniprovska substation and 750 kV line are essential components of the ZNPP's energy infrastructure.

Diesel fuel at the ZNPP

The four emergency diesel generators in automatic standby at the ZNPP, out of a total of 19 available emergency diesel generators, started automatically when power was lost. Two have since been shut down to conserve diesel fuel. To further conserve diesel fuel reserves during this period, the plant has suspended on-site heating, despite temperatures at the site falling to as low as 0°C this week.

The IAEA estimates that the ZNPP has sufficient diesel fuel to maintain its current configuration of two operating emergency diesel generators for more than ten days. The IAEA continues to closely monitor diesel fuel stocks and consumption at the ZNPP.

Over the past months, the Agency has received varying information regarding the availability and location of diesel fuel at the site and is seeking further clarification to independently assess the current diesel fuel situation.

To further optimize diesel fuel use while maintaining essential safety functions, the ZNPP has shut down all reactor heat removal pumps and is currently operating only the spent fuel pool cooling pumps on Units 1 and 6. Coolant temperatures remain within normal operational limits, but are rising, meaning that pumps will need to be periodically restarted to control temperatures within safe limits.

“The diesel fuel conservation measures help the plant deliver its fundamental safety functions. Yet the cold conditions and the decision to only operate safety related equipment periodically underline the challenges facing staff at the site,” said Director General Grossi.

Military activity

The IAEA team at the ZNPP reported hearing military activity every day throughout the week, while the ZNPP alleged that attacks occurred on civilian vehicles on site.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, other nuclear power plants (NPPs) continued to report fluctuations in power output due to grid instability linked to military activity, including the loss of multiple off-site power lines.

Over the past week, a total of 143 air raid alerts occurred. Drones were reported at three of the sites in Ukraine where IAEA staff are present: 10 at the Khmelnytskyy NPP, 26 at the South Ukraine NPP — one of which reportedly passed directly over the plant — and 91 at the Chornobyl NPP. Drones were also reported as close as 100 m to the Centralised Spent Fuel Storage Facility, which is located in the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone.

“I once again call for the end of military activity near all nuclear facilities. As I have said before: no one benefits from a nuclear disaster,” said Director General Grossi.

IAEA assistance to Ukraine

Also this week, under the IAEA’s assistance programme for Ukraine, dose rate meters and a hot water tank were delivered to the National Research Center for Radiation Medicine. Air handling units and air conditioners were provided to the Chornobyl NPP, while filtering polymeric fibrous material was delivered to the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center and related organizations of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine. These deliveries were made possible through funding provided by Japan.

items.title: Sudan: Plus de 380 000 personnes déplacées dans la région du Kordofan au Soudan alors que la violence pousse des milliers d'autres à fuir
items.blurb:
Country: Sudan
Source: International Organization for Migration

Khartoum, 26 novembre 2026 – Plus de 383 000 personnes ont été déplacées de la région du Kordofan au Soudan entre octobre 2025 et octobre 2026, une recrudescence de l'insécurité ayant contraint 15 000 personnes supplémentaires à fuir en novembre seulement. L'Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM) avertit que des vagues successives de déplacements aggravent une crise humanitaire déjà sévère, laissant des milliers de familles sans abri sûr, sans accès aux services de base ni aux moyens de subvenir à leurs besoins.

« Des familles à travers le Kordofan sont contraintes de fuir à maintes reprises, tandis que les communautés qui les accueillent peinent déjà à satisfaire leurs propres besoins essentiels », a déclaré Mohamed Refaat, Chef de mission de l'OIM au Soudan. « Les civils doivent être protégés. À mesure que davantage de personnes sont forcées de quitter leur foyer, nous avons urgemment besoin de ressources et d'un accès sécurisé pour les atteindre avant que leur situation ne se détériore encore davantage. »

Le Kordofan occidental a été particulièrement touché par la dernière vague de déplacement. En novembre seulement, la Matrice de suivi des déplacements (DTM) de l'OIM a enregistré 21 épisodes de déplacement dans la région, forçant environ 15 310 personnes à quitter leur foyer. Près de 90 % des personnes déplacées provenaient du Kordofan occidental, dont quelque 12 720 de la seule localité d'Abu Zabad.

De nombreuses familles ont été contraintes de se déplacer à plusieurs reprises, épuisant leurs ressources déjà limitées et perturbant leur accès aux soins de santé, à l'éducation et à d'autres services essentiels. Le nombre croissant de personnes cherchant refuge dans le Kordofan du Nord, le Nil Blanc et Khartoum exerce une pression supplémentaire sur les communautés hôtes et les services essentiels déjà sous pression.

Les conditions humanitaires sont particulièrement préoccupantes dans le Kordofan occidental, où 70 % des ménages interrogés dans le cadre de l'Évaluation multisectorielle des besoins 2026 de l'OIM ont signalé des besoins de protection, tandis que l'accès aux soins de santé et à l'éducation demeurait gravement limité. À travers le Soudan, 38 % des ménages interrogés ont signalé des besoins non satisfaits en matière d'abri. Dans le Kordofan, les déplacements répétés, les dommages causés aux habitations et la perte de biens essentiels ont privé de nombreuses familles d'un abri adéquat et sûr.

L'OIM continue de suivre les déplacements dans le Kordofan et d'autres zones affectées du Soudan afin d'identifier les besoins émergents et d'orienter les efforts de réponse humanitaire. En collaboration avec ses partenaires, l'OIM soutient les efforts visant à fournir une aide humanitaire d'urgence, notamment des abris d'urgence, des articles ménagers essentiels et d'autres services essentiels.

Alors que l'insécurité continue de provoquer des déplacements à travers le Kordofan, l'OIM appelle à la protection des civils et des infrastructures civiles, à un accès humanitaire sûr et sans entraves, ainsi qu'à la mobilisation urgente de financements supplémentaires pour répondre aux besoins croissants. En l'absence d'un soutien immédiat, des milliers de familles supplémentaires risquent de se retrouver sans l'assistance dont elles ont besoin pour survivre.

Notes à l'intention des rédacteurs

  • Au cours du mois de novembre 2026, l'OIM a enregistré 21 épisodes de déplacement dans la région du Kordofan, entraînant le déplacement d'environ 15 310 personnes. Seize de ces épisodes ont été enregistrés dans le Kordofan occidental, où environ 13 515 personnes ont été déplacées. Ces chiffres sont issus des rapports de terrain de la Matrice de suivi des déplacements (DTM) de l'OIM.
  • Les besoins humanitaires cités dans ce communiqué sont tirés de l'Évaluation multisectorielle des besoins au Soudan 2026 de l'OIM (MSNA). Cette évaluation offre une vue d'ensemble des besoins humanitaires dans le Kordofan occidental et ne doit pas être interprétée comme une évaluation des 12 720 personnes récemment déplacées dans la localité d'Abu Zabad.
  • Des informations complémentaires sur les déplacements récents dans la localité d'Abu Zabad sont disponibles via les Alertes rapides DTM Soudan de l'OIM : ville d'Abu Zabad, village d'Abu Galib et plusieurs villages dans la localité d'Abu Zabad.

Les rédacteurs sont invités à utiliser les récentes images de l'OIM en provenance du Soudan pour compléter leur couverture de la crise, disponibles en consultation et en téléchargement sur UNifeed.

Pour plus d'informations, veuillez consulter le Centre médias de l'OIM.

items.title: Sudan: Más de 380 000 personas desplazadas en Kordofán, Sudán, mientras la violencia obliga a miles más a huir
items.blurb:
Country: Sudan
Source: International Organization for Migration

Jartum, 26 de noviembre de 2026 – Más de 383 000 personas fueron desplazadas de la región sudanesa de Kordofán entre octubre de 2025 y octubre de 2026, mientras que la renovada inseguridad obligó a otras 15 000 personas a huir solo en noviembre. La Organización Internacional para las Migraciones (OIM) advierte que las sucesivas oleadas de desplazamiento están agravando una crisis humanitaria ya crítica, dejando a miles de familias sin alojamiento seguro, acceso a servicios básicos ni medios de subsistencia.

"Las familias de todo Kordofán se ven obligadas a huir una y otra vez, mientras que las comunidades que las acogen ya tienen dificultades para satisfacer sus propias necesidades básicas", declaró Mohamed Refaat, Jefe de Misión de la OIM en Sudán. "Los civiles deben ser protegidos. A medida que más personas son expulsadas de sus hogares, necesitamos urgentemente los recursos y el acceso seguro para llegar a ellas antes de que su situación se deteriore aún más".

Kordofán Occidental ha sido especialmente afectado por la última oleada de desplazamiento. Solo en noviembre, la Matriz de Seguimiento del Desplazamiento (DTM) de la OIM registró 21 incidentes de desplazamiento en toda la región, que obligaron a aproximadamente 15 310 personas a abandonar sus hogares. Casi el 90 por ciento de estos desplazamientos se originaron en Kordofán Occidental, con alrededor de 12 720 personas obligadas a huir únicamente de la localidad de Abu Zabad.

Muchas familias se han visto obligadas a desplazarse en repetidas ocasiones, agotando sus ya limitados recursos e interrumpiendo el acceso a la atención sanitaria, la educación y otros servicios esenciales. El creciente número de personas que buscan refugio en Kordofán Septentrional, el Nilo Blanco y Jartum ejerce una presión adicional sobre las comunidades de acogida y unos servicios ya sobrecargados.

Las condiciones humanitarias son especialmente preocupantes en Kordofán Occidental, donde el 70 por ciento de los hogares encuestados en el marco de la Evaluación Multisectorial de Necesidades de la OIM de 2026 indicaron tener necesidades de protección, mientras que el acceso a la atención sanitaria y la educación seguía estando gravemente limitado. En todo Sudán, el 38 por ciento de los hogares encuestados indicaron tener necesidades de alojamiento no satisfechas. En Kordofán, el desplazamiento reiterado, los daños a las viviendas y la pérdida de pertenencias esenciales han dejado a muchas familias sin un alojamiento adecuado o seguro.

La OIM continúa realizando el seguimiento del desplazamiento en Kordofán y otras zonas afectadas de Sudán para identificar necesidades emergentes y orientar los esfuerzos de respuesta humanitaria. En colaboración con sus socios, la OIM contribuye a proporcionar asistencia humanitaria, incluido alojamiento de emergencia, artículos de socorro básicos y otros servicios esenciales.

Ante la inseguridad que sigue impulsando el desplazamiento en todo Kordofán, la OIM hace un llamamiento a la protección de la población civil y las infraestructuras civiles, al acceso humanitario seguro y sin obstáculos, y a la aportación urgente de financiación adicional para atender las necesidades crecientes. Sin un apoyo inmediato, miles de familias más corren el riesgo de quedarse sin la asistencia que necesitan para sobrevivir.

Notas para los editores

  • Durante noviembre de 2026, la OIM registró 21 incidentes de desplazamiento en toda la región de Kordofán, que afectaron a un estimado de 15 310 personas. Dieciséis de estos incidentes se registraron en Kordofán Occidental, donde aproximadamente 13 515 personas fueron desplazadas. Las cifras se basan en los informes de campo de la Matriz de Seguimiento del Desplazamiento (DTM) de la OIM.
  • Las necesidades humanitarias citadas en este comunicado provienen de la Evaluación Multisectorial de Necesidades de Sudán de 2026 (MSNA) de la OIM. La evaluación ofrece una visión más amplia de las necesidades humanitarias en Kordofán Occidental y no debe interpretarse como una evaluación de las 12 720 personas desplazadas recientemente en la localidad de Abu Zabad.
  • Puede consultarse información adicional sobre el desplazamiento reciente en la localidad de Abu Zabad a través de las Alertas Rápidas de la DTM de la OIM en Sudán: ciudad de Abu Zabad, aldea de Abu Galib y múltiples aldeas en la localidad de Abu Zabad.

Se alienta a los editores a utilizar material audiovisual reciente de la OIM procedente de Sudán para complementar su cobertura de la crisis, disponible para su visualización y descarga en UNifeed.

Para más información, visite el Centro de Prensa de la OIM.

items.title: World: Routes Monitor Key Updates - November 2026
items.blurb:
Countries: World, Algeria, Bangladesh, Eritrea, Italy, Malaysia, Myanmar, Spain
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Highlights

1. The Central Mediterranean Route recorded a moderate increase in September, driven by sea arrivals to Italy. Italy registered 3,329 arrivals, 11% more than in August, but 60% fewer than in September 2025. Nationality patterns also shifted : compared with September 2025, when Bangladeshis and Egyptians predominated, the September 2026 profile was led by Algerians, Eritreans, Bangladeshis and Somalis.

2. Arrivals to Spain increased in September, driven by a rise in arrivals to the Canary Islands in the Western Africa Atlantic Route. Spain recorded 4,229 arrivals during the month, 27% more than in August and 24% more than in September 2025. Arrivals along the Western Africa Atlantic Route increased from 488 in August to 1,970 in September, while arrivals to mainland Spain and the Bale aric Islands along the Western Mediterranean Route declined from 2,832 to 2,259. In Algeria, disembarkations following interceptions or rescue operations increased moderately, from 686 in August to 788 in September, but remained below the 1,405 recorded in September 2025. Overall, Spain recorded 24,646 sea and land arrivals between January and September 2026, 10% fewer than during the same period in 2025.

3. Maritime movements along the South and South -East Asia Route reached their highest level for the first nine months of any year since systematic tracking began in 2022. Around 6,000 maritime movements were recorded between January and September 2026, alongside an estimated 10,700 land movements. The majority of maritime arrivals occurred along routes between Myanmar and Malaysia, while most estimated land movements were t owards Bangladesh .

MESSAGES CLÉS

• Le coût médian du PMAS a diminué sur l’ensemble des marchés évalués avec une baisse de 10% de son prix par rapport à août. Cette tendance a été principalement observée dans la composante alimentaire, tandis que les coûts des paniers de produits non alimentaires et d’hygiène ont connu une hausse. Cependant les marchés de Bangui-Rapide, Boali et Markounda ont connu une hausse importante de leur PMAS. De manière générale, des disparités ont persisté entre les différents marchés, avec un coût médian du PMAS compris entre 40 014 XAF à Bangassou et 102 702 XAF à Dimbi.

• La fonctionnalité des marchés est demeurée limitée, avec des scores SFM compris entre 51% et 88%. Cette relative stabilité a masqué des évolutions contrastées entre les différentes dimensions, marquées par une stabilité de la disponibilité des produits, un recul de l’abordabilité et une amélioration des circuits d’approvisionnement. Des améliorations des scores SFM ont été observées à Bangassou, Batangafo et Ngaoundaye, tandis que Bossangoa et Koui ont enregistré une détérioration. L’indisponibilité de certains produits et les difficultés liées à leur abordabilité ont été relevées, parallèlement à des contraintes affectant l’accessibilité des marchés et les circuits d’approvisionnement. Malgré ces évolutions, les écarts de fonctionnalité entre les marchés ont persisté, soulignant des conditions de fonctionnement et d’approvisionnement toujours hétérogènes selon les localités.

items.title: World: From forecasts to action: strengthening Africa's response to El Niño
items.blurb:
Countries: World, Malawi
Source: Norwegian Refugee Council

As the latest El Niño threatens extreme weather across Africa, NORCAP climate experts are turning weather and climate data into early community defences.

By Gifty Baah

Published 26. Nov 2026

In Malawi, a farmer listening to a seasonal forecast hears that rainfall is likely to be below normal. But one important question remains unanswered: when should I plant?

Plant too early and seeds may fail if the rains stop. Plant too late and crops may not reach maturity. For millions of farmers across Africa, these decisions determine whether families harvest enough food, earn an income, or face hardship. This gap between climate information and decision-making, is where NORCAP's work makes a difference.

As Africa faces the impacts of the current El Niño event, NORCAP experts embedded in Regional Climate Centres and National Meteorological and Hydrological Services are contributing to transforming climate data into actionable information. Their support is strengthening forecasting systems, building technical capacity, and improving the early warnings that governments, communities and humanitarian agencies rely on to prepare for climate extremes.

What is El Niño?

A continent facing growing climate risk

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern characterised by unusually warm surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean.

It weakens trade winds and shifts rainfall patterns, influencing weather conditions across the globe. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) indicates that the current event is almost certain to persist through February 2027 and is forecasted to reach very strong intensity, peaking towards the end of 2026.

El Niño typically peaks between November and February, increasing the likelihood of heatwaves, drought, heavy rainfall and other extreme weather in many parts of the world. WMO's October update forecasts record sea-surface temperatures in the Central and Eastern Tropical Pacific. Even during a very strong El Niño, impacts can vary substantially between regions and seasons. Scientists stress that El Niño is natural, but its effects are now unfolding on a planet already made much warmer by human-caused climate change.

The contrast from Africa is sharp. ACMAD's September bulletin warns of above normal rainfall and flood risk in the Greater Horn and East Africa, and below normal rainfall in Southern Africa during the main planting season.

  • Floods in West and Central Africa had already affected 1.5 million people in 15 countries by 30th September 2026, displacing 595,000 and killing 533 (OCHA, 2026 as cited by Sandrine).
  • In the Sahel, Climate Impact Lab has projected 66,800 additional heat-related deaths between September 2026 and February 2027 compared with a normal year, with Nigeria (31,400), Sudan (17,500), Niger (10,000) and Chad (8,000) the worst affected.
  • In Madagascar, World Food Programme says 3.7 million people will face crisis-level or worse food insecurity during the October to January lean season (WFP as cited in ACMAD et al., 2026).

Building sustainable local expertise

Accurate forecasts require more than weather stations and technology. They require skilled people and strong institutions capable of turning data into useful information and ensuring it reaches decision-makers and communities.

Across many African countries, national meteorological services continue to face challenges, including limited observation networks, shortages of trained staff, and insufficient resources to maintain and modernise forecasting systems.

NORCAP's contribution focuses on addressing these capacity gaps.

By embedding experts within climate centres and meteorological services, NORCAP helps partners strengthen forecasting capabilities, improve climate products, and enhance early warning dissemination systems. The approach is long-term and sustainable: building local expertise so institutions can continue improving services independently.

The results are already visible. NORCAP's 2025 assessment found that countries using the ClimWeb and CAP Composer platforms issued more than 2,500 per cent more standardised alerts. More than 500 staff from National Meteorological and Hydrological Services received technical training, while the number of African weather stations sharing data internationally increased from 257 to 1,315.

The current El Niño event is demonstrating why these investments matter.

Malawi: Helping farmers make better decisions

In Malawi, NORCAP expert Sinclair Chinyoka has been working with the Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services (DCCMS) to improve the information available to farmers and decision-makers during the current El Niño event. Recognising that farmers need more than broad seasonal forecasts, Chinyoka helped develop a machine-learning system that predicts the likely onset of rainfall and considers how large-scale climate drivers, including El Niño, affect different parts of the country.

He has also strengthened the use of advanced weather-modelling systems to produce localised forecasts and agricultural advisories, while training meteorologists in weather modelling, machine learning and climate forecasting.

"Farmers do not simply need to know whether rainfall will be above or below normal. They need information that helps them decide when to plant, what risks to expect, and how to protect their livelihoods. Our goal is to build national capacity so that these services continue to improve long after our support ends," says Chinyoka.

The improved forecasts are already helping inform national preparedness efforts. Based on seasonal outlooks produced by department, government agencies have developed contingency plans that include drought-tolerant crops, food reserves, livestock support and flood preparedness measures. While implementation depends on available resources, having advance information allows authorities to act earlier and plan more effectively.

ACMAD: Turning climate outlooks into early action

At the continental level, NORCAP experts are supporting the African Centre of Meteorological Applications for Development (ACMAD) to translate climate forecasts into practical guidance for governments, humanitarian agencies and development partners. Through the African Continental Climate Outlook Forum (ACCOF), ACMAD works with regional climate centres and national meteorological services to develop seasonal forecasts and risk information for the continent.

However, forecasting rainfall is only part of the story. For governments, health agencies and humanitarian organisations, the more important question is what those forecasts mean for communities and livelihoods. NORCAP expert Wendalasida Sandrine works with ACMAD and has contributed to strengthening efforts to produce impact-based climate information and guidance that enables action before disasters strike.

"The real value of a forecast is not in predicting the weather. It is in understanding what that weather could mean for crops, water supplies, health systems and vulnerable populations. Our focus is helping decision-makers move from awareness to action," says Sandrine.

NORCAP experts have also supported the development of health-focused seasonal outlooks, strengthened drought-monitoring systems, and helped improve forecasting approaches to make them more objective, robust and reliable. These products are informing preparedness discussions not only among technical agencies, but also at ministerial and policy levels across the continent.

ICPAC: Understanding why risks are emerging

In Eastern Africa, NORCAP supports the IGAD Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC) in enhancing its ability to understand and communicate climate risks. Working through the CRAF'D project, NORCAP-experts developed an innovative forecasting approach that goes beyond showing what might happen, to explain why risks are emerging.

The system combines multiple sources of scientific evidence to assess rainfall hazards, identify key drivers and communicate uncertainty more clearly. For forecasters and disaster managers, this provides deeper insight into evolving risks and supports more informed decision-making. Importantly, recent analyses highlighted that although El Niño increased the likelihood of wetter conditions, rainfall patterns remained uneven in some areas.

The findings reinforced the importance of continuous monitoring and real-time analysis, helping forecasters and disaster management agencies refine their assessments and preparedness measures as conditions evolve.

"Decision-makers need to understand not only what the forecast says, but also how confident we are and what factors are driving the risk," explains Nishadh Kalladath, Data Science and Machine Learning Expert at ICPAC.

"That additional context supports better planning and more informed early action."

From forecast to action

Despite significant progress, experts agree that forecasting is only one part of the solution. The greatest challenge is ensuring that warnings reach communities in time and in forms people can understand and use.

"Producing forecasts is no longer the hardest part. Making sure they lead to action is," says Sandrine.

For farmers, information on the timing of rainfall, dry spells and the end of the season is often more useful than seasonal rainfall totals. Communities also need access to trusted communication channels, local-language advisories, extension services and resources that allow them to act on warnings. NORCAP Regional Adviser, Owiti Zablone, emphasises that climate forecasts should support practical preparedness measures rather than create alarm.

"A forecast is not a prediction of destiny. It is a tool for informed decision-making. When people receive timely, reliable climate information, they can take low-regret actions that strengthen resilience regardless of how the season unfolds," says Owiti.

These actions may include protecting water sources, preparing drainage systems, conserving soil moisture, or adopting drought-tolerant crops.

But climate information alone is not enough.

Farmers also need access to seeds, irrigation, finance and extension support. Communities need warnings delivered through trusted channels and local languages. Governments need systems that connect forecasts to preparedness and response mechanisms.

This is why NORCAP's support focuses not only on improving forecasts, but also on strengthening the institutions and partnerships required to turn information into action.

Investing in resilience before disaster strikes

The current El Niño event is providing a real-world test of Africa's climate services and early warning systems. Across Malawi, ACMAD, ICPAC and many other partner institutions, stronger forecasting capabilities are helping governments and communities better understand risks, prepare earlier and make more informed decisions. The benefits extend beyond this year's El Niño.

Stronger climate services improve food security, support disaster risk reduction, protect livelihoods and contribute to social stability. They also help countries adapt to a future in which climate extremes are becoming more frequent and more intense.

As Sandrine reflects:

"Preparing for El Niño is really about preparing for a more extreme future. Every investment in climate services and early warning systems today is an investment in protecting lives, livelihoods and resilience tomorrow."

items.title: Over 380,000 Displaced from Sudan’s Kordofan as Violence Forces Thousands More to Flee
items.blurb:
Country: Sudan
Source: International Organization for Migration

Khartoum, 26 November 2026 – More than 383,000 people were displaced from Sudan’s Kordofan region between October 2025 and October 2026, with renewed insecurity forcing a further 15,000 people to flee in November alone. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) warns that successive waves of displacement are deepening an already severe humanitarian crisis, leaving thousands of families without safe shelter, access to basic services or the means to support themselves.

“Families across Kordofan are being forced to flee time and again, while the communities taking them in are already struggling to meet their own basic needs,” said Mohamed Refaat, IOM Chief of Mission in Sudan. “Civilians must be protected. As more people are forced from their homes, we urgently need the resources and safe access to reach them before their situation deteriorates even further.”

West Kordofan has been particularly hard hit by the latest wave of displacement. In November alone, IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) recorded 21 displacement incidents across the region, forcing an estimated 15,310 people from their homes. Nearly 90 per cent of these displacements originated in West Kordofan, with some 12,720 people forced to flee Abu Zabad locality alone.

Many families have been forced to move repeatedly, exhausting their already limited resources and disrupting access to healthcare, education and other essential services. The growing number of people seeking refuge in North Kordofan, White Nile and Khartoum is placing additional pressure on host communities and overstretched services.

Humanitarian conditions are particularly concerning in West Kordofan, where 70 per cent of households surveyed as part of IOM’s 2026 Multi-Sector Needs Assessment reported protection needs, while access to healthcare and education remained severely constrained. Across Sudan, 38 per cent of surveyed households reported unmet shelter needs. In Kordofan, repeated displacement, damage to homes and the loss of essential belongings have left many families without adequate or safe shelter.

IOM continues to track displacement across Kordofan and other affected areas of Sudan to identify emerging needs and guide humanitarian response efforts. Working with partners, IOM is supporting efforts to deliver emergency assistance, including shelter, essential household items and other critical services.

As insecurity continues to drive displacement across Kordofan, IOM calls for the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, and urgent additional funding to meet growing needs. Without immediate support, thousands more families risk being left without the assistance they need to survive.

Notes to Editors

  • During November 2026, IOM recorded 21 displacement incidents across the Kordofan region, displacing an estimated 15,310 people. Sixteen of these incidents were recorded in West Kordofan, where an estimated 13,515 people were displaced. The figures are based on IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field reports.
  • The humanitarian needs cited in this release are drawn from IOM’s 2026 Sudan Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA). The assessment provides a broader picture of humanitarian needs in West Kordofan and should not be interpreted as an assessment of the 12,720 people recently displaced in Abu Zabad locality.
  • Further information on recent displacement in Abu Zabad locality is available through IOM DTM Sudan Flash Alerts: Abu Zabad town, Abu Galib village, and multiple villages in Abu Zabad locality.

Editors are encouraged to use recent IOM footage from Sudan to complement their coverage of the crisis, available to view and download on UNifeed.

For more information, please visit IOM’s Media Centre.

items.title: Mozambique Conflict Monitor: Almost 10 years into the insurgency, ISM threatens to expand
items.blurb:
Country: Mozambique
Source: Armed Conflict Location & Event Data

Please refer to the attached file.

ISM’s sustained and increasing presence in Mozambique will significantly impact security sector reform, strategic investments, and the movement of people and goods.

Author

Peter Bofin

Regional Expert, Southeast Africa

Executive summary

As the insurgency in Mozambique enters its 10th year and the end of two years of President Daniel Chapo’s administration draws near, Islamic State Mozambique’s (ISM) actions continue to shape people’s lives across Cabo Delgado province. Despite the continuing presence of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) and the support it provides to the Defense Armed Forces of Mozambique (FADM), in the past two years, ISM has broadened its footprint into Niassa and Nampula provinces, while remaining entrenched in Cabo Delgado’s northeast.

ISM’s increasing activity in the north, south, and west of Cabo Delgado, as well as in Niassa and Nampula provinces, has been driven by three factors: its need to diversify funding, stretch security forces’ limited capacity, and secure supply lines for recruits and other supplies. As ISM has become more dependent on generating its own finances, the most likely outcome is that these trends continue into the insurgency’s 10th year. This will mean continued hindrance to humanitarian work in the province and further postponements in the reconstruction of public administration and economic revival.

Current conflict context

ISM has expanded its operations to become self-reliant

Throughout 2025 and 2026, ISM has become more reliant on financing from artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM), kidnapping for ransom, and extortion on roads. These sources of income have become a financial imperative for the group as external financing has declined due to recent United States and United Arab Emirates airstrikes against the Islamic State (IS) Somalia province, which finances IS internationally.

Recent evidence underscores that the push for self-reliance has been driving ISM’s behavior over the past six months, leading to more frequent activity outside its heartland of Macomia, Mocímboa da Praia, and Muidumbe districts (see map below). To the west, the group was present in the Montepuez and Balama districts in each of the six months from May to October, where it carried out a single operation from July to October. It has also maintained a presence to the south, where it exerted control over gold- and gemstone-producing areas in Meluco and Ancuabe districts, and maintained links to Nampula province through Chiúre district. To the north, it has become increasingly active in Nangade district, along the border with Tanzania, likely to maintain links with support networks north of the border.

ISM is sustaining its presence in the west

In the west, ISM has been active in Montepuez district and has threatened both Niassa province to the west and Balama and Namuno districts to the south. From July through October, it conducted significant operations in Montepuez’s Nairoto area, where it exerted control over ASM gold mining sites, undertook one sortie into Niassa province, and restricted traffic on the R698 road from Montepuez to Mueda by setting up roadblocks (see map below).

This was not ISM’s first sortie to Nairoto. However, its ability to sustain a presence there from July to October suggests it has knowledge and support networks in the area that could support a more permanent presence. The group was based at the Shamba Kubwa gold mining area in the north of Nairoto for most of September and could move freely in Montepuez district and south to Balama district.

ISM’s operations in the west of Cabo Delgado have been its most lucrative thus far. In October, it received over $50,000 in ransom for a South African man the group kidnapped in a raid on a hunting camp in Niassa province the previous month and held in Shamba Kubwa for most of September. According to local sources, much of the ransom was paid in cryptocurrency because the sum was too large for mobile money platforms. Extortion at roadblocks and ransoms paid for Mozambicans captured in village raids are paid through mobile money accounts on Mozambican telecom platforms. ISM’s now-confirmed use of cryptocurrency significantly complicates efforts to control ISM’s access to finance.

The insurgency has maintained its links to Tanzania

To the north, renewed activity in Nangade district in September and October has been modest: ISM has been involved in just seven violent incidents. According to local sources, ISM’s presence is thought to reflect ongoing connections to support networks in Tanzania; the group has been present in the district up to five times each year since 2024. The insurgency has had links to Tanzania since its beginning in 2017, and ISM’s current leader, Sheikh Hassan Ulanga, is originally from Tanzania. Attacks on villages, particularly to the south of the district, regularly displace civilians and place pressure on civic and military authorities, which can create openings for movement of people across the border.

Such movements — which occur along the border in Nangade district and in western Mueda district — likely include active fighters temporarily moving to Tanzania, new recruits coming to Mozambique, and possible cash movements into or out of Mozambique. This continues despite the presence of Tanzanian forces on both sides of the border. Typically, recruits entering Mozambique are met at the border by ISM fighters, before being moved to bases further south.

ISM insurgents target southern Cabo Delgado for gold and recruits

ISM’s behavior in southern Cabo Delgado has been similarly episodic. While not established there, the group undertakes regular violent sorties into the Meluco, Ancuabe, Chiúre, and Namuno districts, as well as into Nampula province (see map below). As in Montepuez, the group has spent significant time south in recent months. Its most significant recent operation lasted two months, and is its longest-lasting operation in the province’s southern districts so far.

As in the west, ISM has multiple objectives in carrying out its operations in the south. First, they allow the group to extort miners and buyers at ASM gold and gemstone mining sites in Ancuabe, Meluco, and Namuno districts. Second, they can help new recruits move north out of Nampula and may serve as a channel for moving gold to markets in Nampula, according to sources in the province.

Movements south are also notable for the sites that ISM does not target. The group does not mount roadblocks on the east-west N1 and N14 roads, nor does it target vulnerable military positions in the south, such as the FADM camp at Macarara close to the N14, or the nearby RDF position at Nacololo. This suggests that ISM has no intention of exerting control over territory between those roads and Nampula, and that its focus is on maintaining links with supporters in Nampula.

State response

State forces, including FADM, the RDF, and the Tanzania People’s Defence Force (TPDF), have not matched ISM’s sustained and distributed activity or its mobility over the past six months. FADM operates under capacity constraints, despite international support. The RDF has had some success with its narrower mandate of ensuring security conditions allow the liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects in the country to proceed. Tanzania’s principal concern of ensuring that the conflict does not spill over its border is an objective it is successfully fulfilling.

FADM carries out limited operations against ISM

FADM’s engagements with ISM have been mostly concentrated in the east, both on land and in nearshore waters, with limited activity to the west, despite ISM’s push into Montepuez and Balama districts from July to October (see map below).

In July, FADM moved the operational command of the Northern Operational Theater of the Defense and Security Forces from Pemba to Mocímboa da Praia. The following month, Mocímboa da Praia’s airport was closed to civilian traffic, though it is still active militarily and provides air support to RDF operations in northern Macomia district. The closure of the airport has significantly restricted humanitarian operations in the town. Despite FADM’s heightened presence, ISM remains active in villages around the town. Both FADM and the RDF are reluctant to respond to the movements of small groups of ISM insurgents in villages around the town and instead focus on breaking up ISM support networks in the town, on which the group depends for food and other supplies.

Most notable is FADM’s lack of engagement with ISM west of the N380 across Macomia and Meluco districts. For ISM, this is strategically important territory. The group targets communities in western Macomia by looting them to support fighters across that district. Meluco is important for two reasons. Firstly, the Messalo River corridor provides access to Montepuez and Balama districts. Secondly, over the past two years, ISM has successfully sought to control artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) in Meluco as a source of income.

International partners: The RDF and TPDF have adopted a less aggressive posture

In the past six months, both the RDF and the TPDF have restricted their activity to areas of greatest strategic interest. The RDF has focused on degrading ISM positions south of Mocímboa da Praia, particularly in the Quiterajo and Mbau area, where ISM maintains a stronghold. Given the RDF’s mission to protect the LNG project further north, its priority is to minimize ISM’s impact on the project’s operations (see map below).

Elsewhere in the province, the RDF has continued to take a less aggressive posture, despite having at least one base on the N380 road in Macomia district and another in Ancuabe district near the N14 road. There, the RDF’s long-standing reluctance to respond to ISM operations continues.

The TPDF is based in Nangade town and Mandimba village, east of Nangade district, and it has at least three positions on the other side of the Mozambique-Tanzania border facing Cabo Delgado. Despite ISM’s increased activity in the Nangade district in recent months, ACLED records just one clash in the past six months between the TPDF and ISM, thought locally to be related to supporting cross-border movements of people and possibly supplies. The TPDF’s quieter posture is consistent with Tanzania’s now-established preference for a less interventionist approach in the region and prioritizing its own domestic security. A consequence of this less interventionist approach is that it doesn’t undermine the status quo.

Outlook

ISM has continued to be adaptive in the past six months, as evidenced in its increasing presence and influence in the west, its more sustained presence in the province’s southern districts, and its continued ability to operate along the Tanzanian border when it chooses to do so. State forces’ response has been less adaptive; FADM, in particular, has been at best reactive in the west, while ignoring the Messalo River corridor. The RDF is restricted in its mandate to remain focused on the east to protect the LNG project in Palma over the long term. This configuration is likely to continue into 2027, with significant consequences for the movement of people and goods, security sector reform, and strategic investments.

ISM poses a threat to the flow of people and goods

The N380 highway, which runs through the heart of the near 10-year-long conflict, will remain open to commercial traffic, though with a high risk that ISM will effectively impose tolls through roadblocks. Driven by commercial interests, businesses will continue to limit exposure to violence on this road through paying off ISM, either at ad hoc roadblocks, which put people and goods at risk, or through anticipatory payments. ISM’s westward move will also make such practices a cost of doing business on the R698, the Montepuez-Mueda route in the west.

The greater impact will be on humanitarian organizations, which have not been in a position to make such arrangements on the N380 and will similarly not be able to do so on the R698. This will restrict support to internally displaced people and returnees in Mocímboa da Praia, Mueda, and Nangade, as well as the revival of public services and the economy in the north.

Security sector reform is necessary to address the ISM threat

Rwanda remains a stable partner and is likely to maintain a presence in Mozambique until at least 2029, the projected year of first production from the TotalEnergies LNG project. FADM and the Ministry of Defense are well-established as the primary points of contact for support, having taken the lead role in the security response from the police in 2021. Nevertheless, security sector reform partners face three key issues that will impact the security response in the coming year as ISM develops a new center of gravity to the west and presents a sustained threat to the north and south.

First, a centralized command structure has slowed troops’ response times in the field. The issue is particularly acute given that ISM prefers to operate in small, mobile groups. Second, there is a need for better intelligence. Finally, logistical and financial obstacles to supporting effective military operations also contribute to slow response times.

These issues will be a priority for international partners such as the European Union and the US government in the coming months. Supporting intelligence-led, decentralized command and control within FADM is a priority for the EU Military Assistance Mission in Mozambique (EUMAMM). If successful, this will likely be reflected in more dynamic FADM action in areas in Montepuez and, if necessary, Niassa, as well as in Cabo Delgado’s southern districts. US support is focused on the police, particularly on improving security on the N380 and the N1 roads. A key indicator of success on these routes will be increased humanitarian traffic, particularly on the N380.

Strategic investments will drive interest in Mozambique

Security sector reform is bound tightly to national and international strategic interests. Northern Mozambique’s natural resources make it of considerable interest to Mozambique itself, its neighbors, and international powers. In 2027, some change can be expected in how these interests are addressed. The critical projects relate to the Eni, TotalEnergies, and ExxonMobil LNG projects. The latter two, being onshore, drive the RDF deployment, while the TotalEnergies-led project is instrumental in European security sector support.

As ExxonMobil approaches its final investment decision on its own onshore LNG project, the US is seeking to expand security sector cooperation through agreed support for the police and proposed support to FADM. If the US gets the green light to undertake Joint Combined Exchange Training in Mozambique in 2027, it will signal heightened US influence with the current administration.

Mining investments will continue to remain at risk. Existing graphite projects in Balama district in Cabo Delgado and Niassa’s Nipepe district will continue. However, as ISM becomes more active in Montepuez, this will pose potential security risks to facilities and main transport routes. As-yet-undeveloped concessions in Balama and Montepuez will likely face considerable delays in attracting financing for development.

If Niassa Reserve boundaries are redrawn to accommodate mining interests, ISM’s continued presence in Montepuez presents a greater threat to Niassa province, threatening existing tourism and conservation interests and potential future mining projects. Finally, more sustained ISM activity in western Cabo Delgado will be most acutely felt by civilian communities, which will become increasingly hard to reach with humanitarian assistance.

It is highly likely that ISM will increasingly gain control of gold resources unless the state can take credible steps to reduce ISM’s influence on the sector through a coordinated approach involving security and other actions such as tackling financing mechanisms and logistics networks.
